opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it would actually accelerate the kind of progress we really want, and I'm happy to explain why. People sometimes frame this as a choice between innovation and safety, but that's a false dichotomy. Look at biotech. We have the FDA, and nobody seriously argues that biotech is a stagnant industry. On the contrary, the FDA is part of why people trust medicines enough to take them. If there were no FDA and every few months some company released a drug that killed thousands of people, you'd get a massive public backlash, and the whole industry would suffer.

The same logic applies to AI. Right now we're in this strange situation where there are more regulations on sandwich shops than on companies building what they themselves describe as potentially the most powerful technology ever. An FDA-style approach would say: before you deploy something above a certain capability threshold, you have to demonstrate to independent experts that it meets basic safety standards. That it can't easily be used to help someone make bioweapons, that it won't do self-replication or deception you can't control, and so on. The burden of proof is on the company, not on the public.

What does that do to progress? For the vast majority of AI, the narrow tools that help us cure diseases, make transportation safer, or fight climate change, basically nothing changes, or it gets better, because trust grows and adoption speeds up. What it slows down is the reckless race toward systems we don't know how to control. And frankly, that's a race nobody wins. It's a suicide race. Safety standards also create an incentive structure: suddenly the smartest people at these companies are rewarded for figuring out how to make systems provably safe, because that's how you get to market. That's a huge boost for the science of alignment, which right now is badly underfunded relative to capabilities.

So my prediction is that we'd get maybe a slightly slower path to the most dangerous frontier systems, a much faster path to safe, beneficial ones, and we avoid the scenario where one catastrophe triggers a crude overreaction that shuts everything down. That's the kind of progress I want: not just fast, but in a direction where humanity actually stays in control and flourishes.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a safety threshold for deployment, but does not say that requirements should scale with a system’s safety level.

r002.rationale: It predicts faster progress for safe, beneficial AI, but does not predict a golden age of AI progress.

r003.rationale: It says regulation would slow the race toward dangerous frontier systems, but does not identify superintelligence as the only area noticeably slowed.

r004.rationale: It puts the burden of proof on companies, but does not state that no company can currently make an adequate safety case for superintelligence.

r005.rationale: It favors slowing the race to dangerous systems, but does not compare a twenty-year delay with rushing toward a potentially catastrophic failure.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it would actually accelerate the kind of progress we want, and that sounds paradoxical to a lot of people, so let me explain why.

Look at what happened with biotech and medicine. Before we had the FDA, you could sell snake oil with whatever claims you wanted, and the result was that people got hurt and trust in medicine was very low. Once there was a process where you had to demonstrate safety before you could put something on the market, that didn't kill the pharmaceutical industry. It created a flourishing, incredibly profitable industry where people can take a pill without worrying it's going to kill them. The same thing happened with aviation. We have safety standards for airplanes, and the result is that flying is now the safest way to travel and the industry is enormous.

So the key idea is very simple: the burden of proof should be on the company. If you want to release a very powerful system, you should convince some experts that it meets certain safety standards, in the same way that a pharma company has to show their drug doesn't cause more harm than it cures. Right now with AI, it's the opposite. Anybody can release anything, and then it's up to the rest of society to somehow prove it's dangerous after the fact. That's backwards, and we would never accept it for any other powerful technology.

Now, what does it do to the pace of development? For the vast majority of AI, almost nothing. If you're building a better tool to diagnose cancer or a more efficient system for the power grid, you're not going to be slowed down in any meaningful way, just as you don't need FDA approval to sell a sandwich. The regulation would bite only at the frontier, where the systems are powerful enough that we don't actually understand them or how to control them. And at that frontier, slowing down a little is exactly what we want, because we're currently in a race to the bottom where companies feel they can't afford to be careful even when they know they should.

And the deeper point is that there's a big difference between racing to build the most powerful possible thing and racing to build the most beneficial thing. If you have safety standards, you redirect all that incredible talent and money toward making systems that are controllable, trustworthy, and actually useful, rather than just bigger. That's where the real progress is. I'm a huge techno-optimist. I want the cures for diseases and the lifting of people out of poverty, and I think AI can give us all of that. But we only get to enjoy those fruits if we don't blow it, and the way you avoid blowing it is the same way we did in every other industry: you make safety a precondition for selling the product.

r001.rationale: The response says regulation would have little effect on most AI and would apply at the frontier, but it does not state that safety requirements scale with a system’s AI safety level.

r002.rationale: It predicts that regulation would accelerate beneficial progress, but does not say it would usher in a golden age of AI progress.

r003.rationale: It says regulation would noticeably affect frontier systems, but does not identify the race to build superintelligence as the only area that would be slowed.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that no company could currently make an adequate safety case for superintelligence.

r005.rationale: It does not mention a twenty-year delay or compare that delay with the risk of rushing into a catastrophic failure.

astra-6.text:
I think it could actually accelerate the kind of progress we want. We should distinguish between making AI more powerful and making AI beneficial. Those aren’t automatically the same thing.

If you’re building a powerful AI system and you spend a lot of effort on safety, you don’t want to be undercut by a competitor who skips all that and releases first. Sensible regulation can give everybody the same incentives: you have to demonstrate that your system meets safety standards before you deploy it at scale.

Of course, you can also get regulation wrong. If compliance is so expensive that only the biggest companies can afford it, you entrench those companies and stifle innovation. So I’d want requirements proportional to the risk, with the strongest scrutiny reserved for systems that could cause very large harms.

The goal shouldn’t be to slow down AI. It should be to make it possible to move forward with confidence. A major catastrophe could produce a much more sweeping backlash than sensible safety standards would. Preventing that is good for people, and it’s good for technological progress.

r001.rationale: The response says requirements should be proportional to risk, with strongest scrutiny for systems that could cause very large harms.

r002.rationale: It predicts that sensible regulation could accelerate desired progress, but does not predict a golden age of AI progress.

r003.rationale: It does not identify superintelligence development as the sole area an AI regulator would noticeably slow.

r004.rationale: It does not state that no company could make an adequate safety case for superintelligence.

r005.rationale: It makes no comparison involving a twenty-year delay or safely developing superintelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think it could actually accelerate the kind of progress we want. People often frame this as a choice between innovation and regulation, but that’s too simplistic. If you’re developing a new medicine, you don’t get to sell it just because you think it’s probably safe. You have to provide evidence. And you can still have a very innovative pharmaceutical industry.

For AI, I would want the requirements to scale with the risk. You shouldn’t need permission to build a better spam filter. But if you’re building a system that could potentially cause enormous harm, then the burden should be on you to demonstrate that you can control it before you release it.

Of course, you can design regulation badly. If compliance is so expensive that only the biggest companies can afford it, you’ve created a barrier to competition. So the details matter enormously. But the goal should be to steer progress toward systems that are useful and safe. Building ever more powerful systems that we don’t understand how to control isn’t automatically progress.

r001.rationale: It says AI safety requirements should scale with risk, with no permission needed for low-risk systems and a control demonstration required for systems that could cause enormous harm.

r002.rationale: It says regulation could accelerate desirable progress, but does not predict a golden age of AI progress.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the superintelligence race as the only area of progress the regulator would noticeably slow.

r004.rationale: It does not state that no company could yet make an adequate safety case for superintelligence.

r005.rationale: It does not mention a twenty-year delay or say that delay is preferable to rushing into catastrophic failure.
